Entries.Text: Show or hide the control instructions in the top-left corner.
Show or hide the profiling information in the top-left corner.
Show or hide the current translation increment in the top-left corner.
Show or hide the current rotation increment in the top-left corner.
Show or hide the viewport tooltip on hover.
Show or hide the placement orb in the viewport.
Show or hide the compass in the viewport.
Open the Tools window at the Camera section of its Rendering tools, which has the view mode, preset views, projection and movement settings.
The view mode, preset views, projection and movement of the current viewport.
How an oblique view draws depth across the screen, and presets for the standard oblique projections.
Reset the camera settings to their defaults.
Show a bar of a round length in the bottom-left corner. In an orthographic view, a metre is the same size everywhere, so the bar measures the whole view.
Draw only a slab of depth around the focus, instead of using the near and far clips. Looking down, it shows one floor of a building as a plan.
Only draw what is within the slice. Alt+mouse wheel changes its thickness; Shift+Alt+mouse wheel moves it nearer or further. Box selection only selects what is in the slice.
The slice's depth in metres, centred on its distance.
How far ahead of the camera the middle of the slice is. Framing a selection puts the slice there.
45 degrees, with depth drawn at half scale. The usual oblique look, with little distortion.
45 degrees, with depth drawn at full scale, so you can measure lengths along every axis.
Looks down with depth at full scale: the ground plan is true to scale, and heights rise up the screen at 45 degrees.
When switching to Oblique, turn the camera to the nearest world axis, because a slanted view from a free rotation is hard to read.
Perspective only: an orthographic camera sits in the middle of what it draws.
Look along a world axis. The camera turns about the last framed point, so it stays in view.
Turn the camera to the world axis nearest its view direction, with the nearest axis as up.
Choosing a view in Perspective switches to Orthographic, and rotating the camera afterwards switches back to Perspective.
Zoom the mouse wheel about the point under the cursor instead of the centre of the view.
The minimum distance at which entities are rendered in the viewport.
The maximum distance at which entities are rendered in the viewport.
Hide the geometry within a radius around the camera, to see through nearby walls and ceilings.
Don't draw models, collision and navmeshes within the camera's clip radius, and don't let clicks select them.
The distance from the camera, in metres, within which geometry is clipped.
The mouse sensitivity for turning the camera.
The camera speed while holding Shift.
The camera speed while holding Ctrl.
This viewport moves at x{0} of these speeds, to suit the scale of what it shows.
The nearest depth drawn, measured along the camera's view from its position. Negative values are behind the camera, which an orthographic view still draws.
The furthest depth drawn, measured along the camera's view from its position. Must be greater than the near clip.
The speed of middle mouse panning. At 25, the scene follows the cursor exactly; lower is slower and higher is faster.
The height of the view in world units (metres). The mouse wheel changes it, and framing a selection sets it.
The screen direction, in degrees, towards which things nearer the camera are drawn: 0 is right and 90 is up. The framed selection stays in place as it changes.
How far depth is drawn across the screen per unit of depth: 0.5 is cabinet, 1.0 is cavalier, and 0 is a plain orthographic view.
Play materials that animate over time in the viewport. When off, they hold their current frame.
How strongly vegetation moves in the viewport. The game's own wind varies by place, so this is an approximation.
The direction vegetation is blown in, in degrees.
Flags, cloth and creatures with baked vertex animations play them.
Hanging objects and leaves sway back and forth.
Flocks of birds flap and fly around their paths.
Materials blend their texture layers. When off, only the first layer is shown.
Materials apply their detail albedo and overlay normal textures.
Magma materials give off their flowing glow.
Materials give off light from their emissive textures.
Sky, clouds and flames are drawn unlit. This stands in for the game's shaders, which depend on its scene.
Water gets moving ripples and a smooth surface. This stands in for the game's shaders, which depend on its scene.
Fur is cut out into strands instead of being drawn as solid cards.
Light models inside environment boxes with the map's baked irradiance volumes instead of the environment map. Outside every box, models keep the environment map's light.
The volumes' light is in the game's own units. Auto exposure scales it so the volumes' average matches the viewport's default ambient light. Current exposure: {0:F1}
Multiply the volumes' light. With Auto Exposure off, this is the exposure itself; about 25 matches typical maps.

The irradiance volume bake to light the maps with: the NN of the map's envmap_NN files. Bakes are probably times of day; most Nightreign maps only have bake 0. A change applies the next time a map loads.

Blend the volumes' light towards a second bake, as the game does between times of day. The second bake's textures load with the map, so turning this on or changing the bake applies the next time a map loads.
The bake to blend towards. Volumes that don't have it keep the first bake's light.
How far to blend towards the second bake: 0 is the first bake and 1 the second. Applies immediately.

Scale the environment map's reflections by how bright the volumes' light is at each point compared with the volume's average, as the game does, so reflections darken in shadow and brighten in lit areas.

Take the sun's direction, colour and intensity, the hemisphere ambient light and the exposure from the map's GPARAMs, as the game does. The irradiance volumes then use the same exposure instead of their auto exposure, and the hemisphere replaces the grey environment map for ambient light and reflections. With several maps loaded, the first (by name) with its own GPARAM lights them all.

Multiply the GPARAM's exposure. Most maps turn on the game's auto exposure, which adjusts the exposure to what is on screen. Smithbox uses the GPARAM's value unchanged, so some maps may look too bright or too dark.

The GPARAM's hemisphere light (sky colour from above, ground colour from below) lights what the irradiance volumes don't cover, and the reflections. With this on, it also adds to the volumes' light, which matches the game.
Light DS3's map pieces with their lightmaps (the DOL textures of gi_env) instead of the light probes, as the game does. Applies to maps loaded after the change.

Light Demon's Souls map pieces with their baked lightmaps (the g_Lightmap textures) instead of the ambient light. Layered materials have no room for the lightmap's UV set, so they go without. Applies to maps loaded after the change.
The viewport's scale for the lightmaps' light. How the game scales them is unknown, so compare the map pieces with the game (or with the light-probe-lit objects next to them) and report the value.

Draw one part of the map lighting instead of the lit image. Source: where each surface's ambient light comes from: green a lightmap, blue light probes or irradiance volumes, red the hemisphere, and yellow a lightmapped material whose part found no lightmap. Ambient: that light alone, without the surface's colour. Sun Mask: how much sun each surface lets through, from white (all) to black (none).
Light with {0}, the GPARAM chosen by the selected collision's scene GPARAM (its sub ID N picks mAA_BB_0N00), as the game does while the player is on it.
Select a collision whose scene GPARAM sub ID has a file in its area, to light with that GPARAM.

Light with a weather, by its GparamId in WeatherParam: the area's own version of the GPARAM (mAA_BB_CCWW) where one exists, with the shared outdoor overlays m00_00_WWWW_weatheroutdoor and _weatherbase over it, which rain and snow change.

Read the weather's shared overlays (m00_00_WWWW_weatheroutdoor, then _weatherbase) before the map's own GPARAM, as the game does outdoors. Their light, tone map, fog and Wet values replace the map's. Turn off for interiors.
Time {0}: the GPARAMs' key for this timezone. In Elden Ring it is also the time irradiance volume bake {1} was made at.
Irradiance Volumes Follow the Time of Day

Light with the irradiance volume bakes for the time of day, blending between the two timezones on either side, as the game does (bake N is timezone N). The bakes a time needs load when the time reaches them, unless every bake is loaded with the map (see below).
Load Every Bake with the Map

Load the irradiance volumes for every time of day when a map loads, so you can change the time without waiting. Each bake uses hundreds of MB of GPU memory on a large map. When off, a map loads only the current time's bakes, and the others load when the time reaches them. Applies to maps loaded after the change.
The bakes follow the time of day (Map Lighting): bake {0} towards {1} by {2:0.##}.
Light Characters with the Model Set

Light characters (c####) with the GPARAM LightSet's model set (ID {0}) instead of the scene's: its own sun, the fill lights (Light 1, which can turn with the camera, and the local lights) and its hemisphere. Not yet compared with the game, so it is off by default.
Fill the viewport background with the BG colour of the map's GPARAM (Setting Info), at the GPARAM's exposure, instead of the background colour from the settings.
No loaded map has its own GPARAM, so the viewport's own sun is used.
The sun comes from the map's GPARAMs (the Map Lighting tab).
Light with the Lights Near the Camera
Light the viewports with the loaded maps' BTL lights near the camera, nearest first. When off, only selected lights shine. Selected lights always shine, wherever they are.
The maximum distance from the camera at which a light still shines.
Only light with lights within their own EnableDist of the camera, as the game turns them on. An EnableDist of 0 means no limit.
The maximum number of lights shaded at once, keeping the nearest. Every pixel checks each of them, so lower this if the viewport slows down.
Not used while the map's GPARAMs light the viewport: the lights' power is in the game's units, so it uses the GPARAM's exposure ({0:0.###}), like the sun.
Lighting with {0} of the {1} lights in range.
Not used while the map's GPARAMs light the viewport: the volumes use the GPARAM's exposure, like the sun.

The GPARAM where each value is looked up first. Values it doesn't have come from mapbase, then default.
You can choose any of the project's GPARAMs; one from another area lights every loaded map.
The time on the GPARAMs' TimeOfDay scale. Elden Ring keys its lighting at 0, 4, 8, 12, 15, 21 and 22.5, where 0 is morning, 12 evening and 15 night.
Volumes in the shading table: {0} of {1}
The linked environment boxes whose four bake textures are on the GPU. Boxes the game skips are left out.
{0}: {1} volumes in bake {2}, {3} of {4} environment boxes linked
Environment boxes without a volume: {0}. Skipped by the game: {1}
Open the Irradiance Volumes tab of the Validation tools, which lists each environment box's volume and can fill in their volume ID property from their names.

Hold Ctrl while dragging the gizmo to snap.

Rotation snaps to steps of this many degrees (0 to disable). Translation snaps to the squares of the grid shown in the Grid Configuration tool, while that grid is visible.
Set the gizmo to Translate mode.
Set the gizmo to Rotate mode.
Set the gizmo to Scale mode.
Place the gizmo origin using the selection's local position.
Place the gizmo origin using the selection's world position.
Orient the gizmo origin using the world position.
Orient the gizmo origin using the bounding box.
Draw surfaces fullbright, with their textures unlit. Map lighting, global illumination, shadows, fog and post effects are off, whatever the Rendering tool says.
Light the scene as the game does. Map lighting, global illumination, shadows, fog and post effects follow the Rendering tool's settings.
Show the surfaces' normals instead of the image (the Normals surface view).
Draw lines along the triangles of FLVER models, over their surfaces or by themselves. Selected models draw their lines in the selection colour instead of an outline.
Leave out the surfaces, so only the lines show and you can see what is behind between them. Faces turned away from the camera are still left out.
How much the lines cover the surfaces under them. Lines Only draws them fully opaque.
The width of the lines in pixels, the same at any distance.
Cull objects outside the camera frustum in the viewport.
Light models with the baked irradiance volumes. When off, they use the ambient light from outside the volumes. This is the same setting as the Global Illumination tab of the Rendering tool.

Light the viewports with the map's GPARAM lighting: its sun, hemisphere, exposure, tone map and background. When off, the Scene Lighting tab's own sun and settings are used. This is the same setting as the Map Lighting tab of the Rendering tool.
Make the sun cast shadows. When off, the shadow maps aren't drawn. This is the same setting as the Shadows tab of the Rendering tool.
Try to hide model masks using each entity's NpcParam flags.
How far in front of the camera the placement orb is.
The angle offset used to determine which direction is north.
The radius of the dummy polygon mesh.
The radius of the node mesh.
The size of the dummy polygon ID and bone name text in the viewport.
Choose which models load with a map.
Choose which textures load with a map.

Hold a mouse button in the viewport to control the camera.
Use WASD to move.
Right-click and drag to rotate the camera.
Hold Shift to temporarily speed up, or Ctrl to slow down.
Scroll the mouse wheel to adjust the overall speed.
Numpad 7, 1 and 3 give the top, front and right views; add Alt for the opposite view.
Hold Ctrl+Alt and left-click to make a box selection.

Hold a mouse button in the viewport to control the camera.
Pan with the middle mouse button.
Right-click and drag to rotate the camera.
Scroll the mouse wheel, or use W and S, to zoom.
Use A, D, Q and E to move across the view.
Framing a selection zooms to fit it.
Numpad 7, 1 and 3 give the top, front and right views; add Alt for the opposite view.
Numpad 9 snaps to the nearest axis, and Numpad 5 cycles the view mode.
Numpad 0 toggles the slice; Alt+mouse wheel sets its thickness, and Shift+Alt+mouse wheel moves it.
Hold Ctrl+Alt and left-click to make a box selection.

How the viewport's HDR scene is mapped to the screen. From GPARAM uses the map's Tone Map group under map lighting: ToneMapMode 8, which every Elden Ring GPARAM uses, is a Reinhard curve whose white point is the Reinhard Contrast times the Reinhard White Balance, and 7 is the filmic curve. This approximates the game's curves, and anything without map lighting is clipped. Clamp clips at white, as the viewport did before it had an HDR target.
Multiply the scene before the curve. The GPARAM's exposure is already applied to the map's lighting, so this is added on top.
The brightness that the Reinhard curve maps to white, when the curve is set to Reinhard. From GPARAM uses the map's own value.

Shadows cast by the sun, in up to four cascades. Under map lighting, the cascade splits, far fade and bias come from the map's GPARAM Shadows group; otherwise, from Elden Ring's mapbase. Only models drawn with the full material shader cast and receive shadows.
The size of each cascade's shadow map. The four cascades share one map twice this size on each side, per viewport.
How much sunlight a shadow blocks: 1 blocks all of it.
Multiply the GPARAM's Depth Bias and Slope Scaled Depth Bias. Raise it if surfaces shade themselves in stripes; lower it if shadows separate from what casts them.

Make parts cast shadows as set by their IsShadowSrc or IsShadowOnly, and receive them as set by their IsShadowDest (ShadowSource and ShadowDest in DS3 and Bloodborne; in Elden Ring, the Is Sun Shadow Source, Is Shadow Only and Is Shadow Destination flags, each only when its override is on). Otherwise, every part does both. Applies to parts as they are loaded or edited, so reload the map to apply it to all of them.
The map whose GPARAM lighting and irradiance bake light this editor's viewports, because it has no map of its own. Lit with: {0}. Shared by the Model and Time Act Editors.
The project has no map to borrow lighting from.
The irradiance volume of the map's bake to light with. Automatic picks the one whose average light is the map's median, among those with the most bakes.

The size of the box the volume is stretched over, centred on the origin. The volume's own box isn't read, so this isn't the game's scale. A smaller box shows more of the volume's variation across the model.
The map has no irradiance volumes.

Draw the screen effects of the map's GPARAMs between the scene and the tone map: bloom, fog, light shafts and others, each with its own switch once drawn. When off, the scene goes directly to the tone map.
No screen effects are drawn. They need the map's lighting (Map Lighting tab), and FXAA needs its switch.

Where the GPARAM's Tone Map turns on auto exposure, adjust the exposure to what is on screen: by Middle Gray minus the scene's mean log2 light, within Adaption Min to Max, at the adapt speeds. When off, the GPARAM's Exposure is used unchanged.
Auto exposure: scene mean {0} (log2), adjusted {1} EV towards {2}
The scene's mean is in the game's light units, before any exposure. If the image looks too dark or bright compared with the game, report these numbers with the map and time.
Where the GPARAM's Bloom group is on, blur what is brighter than Glare Threshold over Glare Num Levels levels, and add it at Bloom Alpha.

Smooth jagged edges after the tone map, with the GPARAM Anti-Alias group's FXAA values (Elden Ring's mapbase without map lighting). Used for every Anti-Alias Type except TAA (5), and for TAA too when TAA is off.

Where the GPARAM Anti-Alias group's type is TAA (5, Elden Ring's mapbase), draw the scene a sub-pixel off each frame over JitterCount frames, blend it into a history by Feedback Weight (less with depth), and sharpen it by Sharpen Intensity. Smooths edges, grass and SSAO/SSR noise while the camera is still. Replaces FXAA.

Where the GPARAM's VolumetricFog group is on, haze the scene with its height fog out to Far Depth (and to Fog End Depth with Enable Analytical Fog), lit by the Sky Light and Dir Light colours. Needs map lighting.

Make transparent FLVERs (water, glass, foliage cards) fog themselves at their own depth with the same fog, because they are drawn over the fogged scene. Alpha-blended ones also get the fog's light; additive ones are only dimmed.
Shade the fog's sunlight with the sun's shadow maps, which creates shafts of shadow through gaps. Needs Shadows on.

In a weather whose WeatherParam makes things wet (Wet Time above 0), surfaces facing the sky darken towards the GPARAM Wet group's Override Albedo and become glossier towards Override Shininess, by Albedo Rate and Shininess Rate; walls change half as much. Needs a weather and Outdoor Weather.

Keep surfaces under roofs, arches and tree canopies dry, using a top-down depth map of the scene covering 256 m around the camera. It is redrawn when the camera moves 32 m or the map's models change. Outside that square, everything facing the sky is wet.
Rain mask: around x {0}, z {1}, drawn {2} times
Where the map of what the rain reaches was last centred. The count should only increase when the camera moves 32 m or models load, not every frame.

Where the GPARAM's LightShaft group is on, fan rays out from the sun where the sky shows around it, coloured by Sky Multiply Color and Sky Add Color, whose intensity (w) is 0 at many times of day. Needs map lighting.

Show what the screen space effects read instead of the image: the normals, roughness and specular of opaque FLVERs as they are, or the tone-mapped indirect diffuse light. Pixels that no FLVER drew are dark grey.

Where the GPARAM's Glow Filter is on (Elden Ring's mapbase, so every map), blur what surfaces emit (emissive textures, magma) over Glow NumLevels levels and add it around them, however bright the scene is. Only opaque models glow. Needs map lighting.
The viewport's own scale for the glow, on top of the GPARAM's Blur RgbScale. 1 is the GPARAM's value as read.

The viewport's own scale for the bloom, on top of the GPARAM's GlareBloom Alpha and the game's own scale (Sekiro 0.5, matched against the game). 1 is the game as matched. The game sets part of its bloom strength in its code, which is unknown, so if a game's bloom looks too strong or weak, adjust this to match and report the value.

The viewport's own scale for the fog density, on top of the GPARAM's (already divided by its GameScale, which Sekiro sets to 1-12) and the game's own scale (Sekiro 0.1, matched against the game). 1 is the game as matched. If a game's fog looks too thick or thin, adjust this to match and report the value, with the time of day and the game scale shown in the Post Effects table.

Where the GPARAM's SSR group is on, make glossy surfaces reflect what is on screen instead of the environment, with its reject thresholds, ray steps and fades (all Elden Ring maps use mapbase's). Where a ray finds nothing, the environment reflection stays. Water and glass, which are transparent, aren't reflective yet. Works with or without map lighting.
How much of the environment reflection SSR replaces where its rays hit: 1 replaces all of it (as read from the GPARAM), and 0 none.

Darken the ambient light in creases and where surfaces meet, with the GPARAM SSAO group's values (all Elden Ring maps use mapbase's). Only indirect light is reduced, so sunlit faces keep their sunlight. Works with or without map lighting.
The viewport's own scale for how much SSAO darkens, on top of the GPARAM's AO Scale and AO Offset. 1 is the GPARAM's value as read.
Add the map's lights near the camera to the fog, by Local Light Scale, over their range times Local Light Dist Scale.
middle gray {0}, adapting {1} to {2} EV at {3} / {4}
{0} levels, final scale {1}, RGB scale {2}, alpha scale {3}
from {0}, sky mask {1} rad, blur {2} x {3}
density {0} + {1} x exp(-{2} x (y - {3})), levelling off at 2 x {1} below {3}; over game scale {5}; scattering g {4}
scale {0}, offset {1}, kernel {2} to {3} px, fading from {4} m
shininess over {0}, fresnel over {1}, fade to viewer {2}

Where the GPARAM's ColorGrading group is on, pass the image through the LUT named by its LutSourceId, from the maps' mAA_cgrading textures, blending between the two LUTs on either side of the time of day. Needs map lighting.
Reset the clipping distances, field of view, sensitivity, move speeds, pan sensitivity, orthographic size and oblique settings to their defaults.
How fast the camera turns and moves.
Switch to Game render mode to change these:
In Game mode, this game's maps are shown with their BTL lights only:

How much of the viewport's sun and environment map ambient lights the map under its BTL lights, because this game's maps are shown with their BTL lights only. 0 leaves only the BTL lights; 1 is Editor mode's full base light.
Open the Viewport Rendering section of the tool window, which has every lighting, shadow, post effect and material setting.
The direction the sun shines in.
Multiply the direct light: the sun and the other lights.
Multiply the indirect light: the ambient and environment light.
Multiply the brightness of the whole scene.
A point light that follows the camera, for seeing into dark interiors.
How many grass blades are drawn. Changing it rebuilds the grass, so it applies when you release the slider.
Editor render mode turns off everything except layer blending, the shader types, grass and collision opacity. Switch to Game mode to change the rest.
What the viewport is currently drawing. Click the eye to show or hide this section in every tab.
For each loaded map, the values its GPARAMs give and the file each comes from. Click the eye to show or hide this section in every tab.
Debug views. Click the eye to show or hide this section in every tab. It is always shown while a debug view is on.
How the maps' GPARAM lighting is used.
Which GPARAM file and weather the lighting is read from.
Which rows of the map area's DrawParam banks (param/drawparam/aAA_drawparam) the lighting is read from. Demon's Souls has no GPARAM: its map parts pick their rows by their LightID and ToneMapID.
No loaded map has DrawParam lighting.
The LightBank row that lights the viewport: the sun (light 0), the fill lights (1 and 2), the specular colour and the hemisphere. By default, the row most of the map's pieces use.
The ToneMapBank row for the exposure, its adaptation and the bloom. By default, the row most of the map's pieces use.
Light with the rows {0} picks: LightBank {1}, ToneMapBank {2}, ShadowBank {3}, ToneCorrectBank {4}, FogBank {5}.
The FogBank row for the distance fog: where it begins and ends, how thick it gets, and its colour. By default, the row most of the map's pieces use.
Draw the FogBank row's distance fog over the opaque draws. Demon's Souls' fog is often close (tens of metres), so it can hide much of a map at a distance.
Fog: from {0} m to {1} m, density {2}, colour {3}
Light Parts by Their Own LightID

Light each map piece, object and character with the LightBank row its own LightID picks, as the game lights each part, instead of lighting them all with one row. The exposure, shadows, fog and tone correction stay the map's. Choosing a Light Bank row below lights everything with that row instead.
{0} parts lit by {1} rows of their own; the rest by the map's row.
Off while a Light Bank row is chosen: that row lights everything.
Light Map Materials by Env Cubemaps

Light the map's materials like the game's HemEnv shaders (MTD g_LightingType 3): by the hemisphere and the LightBank row's env cubemaps from the area's mAA_9999.tpf, without the sun. Characters and equipment (g_LightingType 1) keep the row's three lights. When off, every material is lit by the sun.
Env: diffuse {0} x {1}; specular {2} x {3}; {4} of 5 cubemaps loaded

Light the viewport with the map's Light events, as the game does: each at the region whose index is its PointLightID, with the colour, strength and reach of the PointLightBank row named by its Point Light Bank ID (-1 is no light). They share the BTL lights' camera radius and limit; a selected event or region lights wherever it is.
Select a map part to light with the rows it picks.

The ShadowBank row for the shadows: their own light direction (not the sun's), how dark they are, and how far from the camera they reach. Demon's Souls' shadows are short, often ending 10 to 60 m away. By default, the row most of the map's pieces use.
The ToneCorrectBank row for the colour correction: brightness and contrast per channel, saturation and hue. By default, the row most of the map's pieces use.
Return every bank to the rows most of the map's pieces use.
Apply the ToneCorrectBank row's colour correction to the final image.
Shadows: light {0}, density {1}, from {2} m, fading from {3} m to {4} m
Tone correction: brightness ({0}), contrast ({1}), saturation {2}, hue {3}
Which map and irradiance volume the lighting is borrowed from.
The hour the GPARAMs are read at.
The viewport's own sun, used when map lighting doesn't provide one.
Scales applied on top of the scene's light.
A light that follows the camera.
How the irradiance volumes light the scene.
Which of the volumes' bakes is used, and whether two are blended.
Whether the loaded maps' EnvMapEffectBoxes are linked to a volume.
Which of the loaded maps' BTL lights are used.
How bright the BTL lights are.
How the HDR scene is mapped to the screen.
The screen effects the maps' GPARAMs request.
Exposure, bloom, glow and colour grading.
Wetness, ambient occlusion and screen space reflections.
The material and vertex animation the shaders play.
The material features drawn on surfaces.
The special shaders some materials use.
The wind the swaying materials follow.
How grass and collisions are drawn.

The Gparam Editor lights its map with the GPARAM selected in its file list, including unsaved edits. Pick the map in the Viewport Preview section. The weather and time of day are the Map Editor's, so both editors light a map the same way.
Following the selected value's time of day: {0}.
Show the active map (the map shown in the content tree, where new objects go) in the viewport overlay.
